sections.content: You know *no solo… sino también* and *tanto… como* from B1 Unit 40, and *no es que… sino que* from B2 Unit 5. A balanced sentence puts two ideas in the same shape, so the reader sees at once how they relate. Three patterns do most of the work.

sections.title: Three balanced patterns
rows: No es un problema de dinero, sino de tiempo.
It is not a problem of money but of time.
Tanto los estudiantes como los profesores aprobaron el plan.
Both the students and the teachers approved the plan.
Ni el precio ni la distancia le importan.
Neither the price nor the distance matters to him.

sections.title: Long and short
sections.content: Rhythm is the second tool. A long sentence with several clauses, followed by a short one, gives the reader a pause and makes the short sentence stand out: *Aunque el plan es caro, ofrece ventajas y se puede pagar en cuotas. Es una buena idea.* Three short sentences in a row sound like a list; one long sentence after another is tiring. Mix them.

With *ni… ni…* before the verb, do not add *no*: *Ni el precio ni la distancia importan*. After the verb you need it, as in A2 Unit 31: *No importan ni el precio ni la distancia*. The two parts of each pattern must have the same shape: *de dinero… de tiempo*, not *de dinero… que es el tiempo*.
